body.p: Three brothers Lapta.[OSV:] "Lapta" - a proper Nenets name, 'lapta' in Nenets means 'a plain'. There lived a mother and her son [together]. The son grew to a man. The son did not know his father when he died. One day the son told his mother: "Mother, show me where my father's reindeer are". The mother and the son had so many reindeer that [those] ate earth instead of moss. Their skin was like fish skin. To scrape them they were going to shepherd them home. The mother says: "Where are you going to with the reindeer?" The son says: "I won't go anywhere. As I am bored here, I'll take a look down the tundra. The mother kept her wits. She untied the sledge, put out the thick reindeer lasso so thick as a handle of a wooden scoop. She suggested the following to the young man: "Down there among the reindeer there are three speckled bucks. Catch the buck that is a little bit bigger than this one. Those [two] will come by themselves bawling. The young man collected the half of the rope. So he went down (to the reindeer). Having looked for the buck his mother was talking about, he caught it. He brought it upwards to harness it. [He saw] that meanwhile his mother had put out a sledge that seemed [to be made] of thirty mammoth tusks and legs. The young man started to harness the sledge. He saw two other speckled bucks, the smaller ones, were coming by themselves bawling. The young man finished to harness the sledge. The mother gave [him] a stick (narapo)[OSV:] "narapo" - a long wooden pole used to drive a deer sledge. made of seven mammoth joints and horns. [His mother] put [him] a speckled patterned fur coat[OSV:] clothing of the deer skin with the fur inside. on. [She] put [him] a new patterned Nenets [coat?] on. Then [his] mother asked him the following: "Don't touch the head of the reindeer. They will carry [you] (on their backs) and [they] will bring you home". The young man untied the reins, sat down and let the reindeer go headfirst. Then he was going forward sooner or later. He sat down on one of the tundra hills. Sitting there he saw three tents standing down on the river shore. Nenets reindeer were running near those tents. The boy kept his wits and drove with his sledge to the tents. [He saw] a pretty big tent standing in the middle. He stopped opposite to those big tents. He stops and sits inside his sledge. People went out of their tents. An old man came up to the young man and said: "What land are you from?" The young man said: "I don't know humans, I don't know anyone. [I'm] from the land where I lived alone. And what kind of man are you?" That old man says the following: "We are the three white rich brothers, the biggest [=oldest] white rich man is me". There he saw how the other people in the street started to catch a reindeer. Among those reindeer they were trying to catch a hornless, Nenets, barren doe. The young man was watching [how] they couldn't catch it. As the boy was sitting inside the sledge collecting the rope, the doe ran near his sledge chased by people. The young man let the doe come closer and caught it, hardly had he pulled the rope, it cut off the doe's [neck]. The young man collected the rope. He said: "Why did I spread blood on the rope?" Those people skinned that reindeer. The Nenets started to eat raw, frozen meat outside. They brought the young man: "Hey, try raw, frozen meat with us". The young man said: "I cannot eat raw, frozen meat". That white rich man said: "Why are you sitting? Put the meat into the tent and cook it". The young man saw how a girl went out of a tent. The girl went out, cut the meat and brought it into the tent. That old man and the young man were sitting for a while and [then] they entered the tent. The young man entered the tent and wanted just to stay in the door. The old man said: "Don't you see the man? Let him forward, why are you keeping him standing in the door?" They let the young man forward and offered [him] a seat near the old man. They took out meat and put [out] diverse food. Two men went outside and brought the spirit into the tent. They started to drink it and to eat. During the meal the young man heard the following: Apparently, three Lapta brothers (came?) to the white rich brothers to woo her [the bride]. The white rich brothers had a sister. They came to woo her. They ate good and went out to leave in different directions. Seemed like they came to an agreement. The next day they would seat the couple together. As the men were going away, the young man also decided to go. As they came outside, while the young man was putting on his fur coat, the eldest Lapta brother told him: "Your fur coat looks like a fish trap[OSV:] a bailer for bailing out fish. and its upper part is like a wooden ladle." The young man didn't say anything [back]. Then he went on. He came home. The mother is standing in the door, waiting for the young man. "Son, where did you go for so long? I was missing you, sitting on this hill." The young man spent the night [there]. The next day he shephered the reindeer home, among them he found two reindeer with cat-like hair, and caught them. He harnessed the sledge without boards.[OSV:] The sledge was harnessed without underlay of boards. He put on an (old?) coat [with fur inside][OSV:] a clothing of deer skin with the fur inside. [KuAI:] also used among Nenets and one [with fur outside]. Whether he took his stick or not, he went on. He came to that tent and saw that Lapta brothers had come earlier. The young man bound the reins and entered the tent. He entered the tent and stayed in the door, as the old man from yesterday said: "Don't you see the poor man? Let him [pass] forward." The young man saw them making room on the seat near the old man. The young man sat down there. He was watching. He saw the engaged couple came, sat down and drank together. The young man also started to drink with those people. The spirit apparently made the young man drunk. The spirit made [him] drunk and he fell down. But would a drunk man know for how long he was lying [there]? At one moment the young man woke up: a man is beating me. Lying like this he heard the sister of those white rich men screaming somewhere: "Hey, what are you looking at!" That young man, who came recently, is being beaten by Lapta brothers. The young man kept his wits. With his elbows he pulled the men lying on him in every which way. He threw them in every which way for the second time and saw, the Nenets Lapta brothers died, some of them torn into parts. He tore some of them in parts in the middle, the youngest wise [Lapta] brother lost his head; the tent lost its poles, its foundation stood without poles. The tent covering[OSV:] "mɔ:tɨkota" - sacking used for covering the tent; "mɔ:tɨkqop" - deer skins with the fur outside used for covering the tent. was lying aside the whole next day. He stood up and saw people gathering together, looking at him. That girl wasn't there. He went [further], opened the tent covering and apparently the girl jumped out of there. The local people stayed there. They built a new tent, drank and ate, and the white rich man married his sister off to the young man. Having placed the married couple together they were drinking for fourteen days. Having placed the married couple together, the white rich brothers moved near to the young man's tent. They lived all together there and still live. That is the end of the tale.
